subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
passage:
Saturday. Parul spread out four lab files and the practical notes. Instead of a bit of each subject every day, all the writing went into this afternoon: aim, procedure, observations, conclusion, one file after another. Yash brought tea and asked why. "Every time I switch from writing to reading, I lose ten minutes remembering where I was," Parul said.

Tuesday. The reading for the two theory papers was done in one long sitting in the library, with all the notes open at once.

Friday. The files were ready before the deadline, the papers had been read, and there had been two clear evenings in between. Yash said it seemed like a real change. Parul was pleased. 😊

qa.q: What went into Saturday afternoon's work?
qa.a: All the lab file writing went into Saturday afternoon, one file after another.

qa.q: Why did Parul want to do all the writing at one time?
qa.a: Parul feels pleased and less scattered, since switching between writing and reading wastes about ten minutes each time and keeping like with like saves effort. 😊

qa.q: What could Parul do if a batch takes longer than planned, and why?
qa.a: Parul could shorten the next batch or move one file to a free evening, since a fixed plan can bend without being dropped.

qa.q: How might Yash see the change in Parul's week?
qa.a: Yash saw that the week had two clear evenings and that the work still got done, which made batching look worthwhile.

grounding: A student groups lab writing on one afternoon and reading on another, saving the effort of switching between kinds of work.
